primer.text: Unstable nuclei shed their excess energy by emitting ionising radiation: alpha particles, beta particles or gamma rays. This note explains why decay happens, what each emission is made of, and how penetration and ionising power set the three apart.

modules.title: Unstable nuclei and radioactive decay
modules.opening: A nucleus is radioactive when a proton-neutron imbalance makes it unstable, and it decays by emitting radiation — a high-energy particle or wave — to reach a more stable state. The emissions are alpha, beta and gamma, and the timing of any single decay is random.
keyPoints: Unstable nuclei have an imbalance of protons or neutrons.
Radioactive decay is the emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus to gain stability.
The emitted radiations are alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays.
Decay events are spontaneous and random — a single nucleus cannot be timed.
Carbon-14 carries two neutrons more than carbon-12, and that imbalance leaves it unstable.

low.restatement: An overloaded nucleus throws out a particle or a burst of energy. That loss leaves it more settled, like letting steam off a pressurised pot.
low.analogy: Radioactive decay is a wobbly stack of blocks toppling a few blocks off — the remaining stack stands steadier.
low.examPointer: The words "random" and "spontaneous" are mark-carrying: no cause, no clock, no prediction for one nucleus.

medium.restatement: Decay releases energy because the daughter arrangement has lower energy than the parent; the emitted particle or photon carries the difference away. Randomness means each nucleus has a constant decay probability per unit time, independent of its history.
medium.analogy: Each unstable nucleus is a lottery ticket with the same tiny winning chance every second — winning (decaying) is unpredictable for any single ticket even though the odds never change.
medium.examPointer: Distinguish radiation (the emission) from radioactivity (the property of the nucleus); questions probe the vocabulary.

modules.title: Alpha, beta and gamma: nature and penetration
sourceHeadings: Penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma
modules.opening: The three radiations differ in what they are and how far they travel. Alpha is a helium nucleus stopped by paper, beta is a fast electron stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium, and gamma is an electromagnetic wave only reduced by thick lead — with ionising power falling in the reverse order.
keyPoints: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus: 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
A beta particle is a high-energy electron created when a neutron becomes a proton.
Gamma rays are the highest-energy electromagnetic waves, with no mass or charge.
Alpha is the least penetrating and the most ionising; gamma is the most penetrating and the least ionising.
Paper stops alpha; a few millimetres of aluminium stop beta; only several centimetres of lead reduce gamma.

low.restatement: Line up three barriers — paper, thin aluminium, thick lead. Alpha dies at the paper, beta dies at the aluminium, gamma ploughs on until lead slows it.
low.analogy: Alpha is a bowling ball (huge impact, barely travels), beta a thrown pebble, gamma a laser beam that goes far but nudges lightly.
low.examPointer: Pair the properties in reverse: most ionising = least penetrating. Questions love that inversion.

medium.restatement: Ionising ability tracks charge and size: the heavy, double-charged alpha rips electrons from atoms most effectively but collides and stops soonest; the massless gamma interacts rarely, so it penetrates furthest while ionising least. Absorber choice follows directly.
medium.analogy: A heavy truck stops at the first wall but wrecks it; a bullet goes further with less smash; a searchlight passes over everything while barely touching it.
medium.examPointer: Absorption tables are free marks if you attach each radiation to its absorber — and remember the beta/aluminium thickness nuance.

glossary.definition: The random emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus, leaving it more stable.
A helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons) emitted from an unstable nucleus.
A high-energy electron emitted when a nucleus converts a neutron into a proton.
A high-energy electromagnetic wave emitted from a nucleus, with no mass or charge.
